passage: From the desk next to hers I watched Disha through the whole exam month. At first she made jokes at the tea break. Then, gradually, she stopped. Her eyes looked tired, her answers to "how are you" were "fine" and "busy," and last Wednesday she snapped at Mehak over a missing pen, which is so unlike her. Mehak looked startled, then quiet. I didn't know what was going on inside Disha; she may have been worn out, or worried about something at home. When she left for lunch, Mehak followed and said something I couldn't hear. They came back together later, Disha's eyes red. Mehak had put a hand on her shoulder. I noticed that the next day Disha stayed home and someone said she'd see a doctor.

qa.q: What did Disha snap at Mehak about?
qa.a: She snapped at Mehak over a missing pen.

qa.q: What might Disha have been feeling in the weeks before she snapped, and what else could explain her manner?
qa.a: She may have been worn out and stressed, showing it through tired eyes and short answers, though something at home could also explain it.

qa.q: What could Mehak and others do for someone who has been under long-lasting strain?
qa.a: They can offer rest, listen and support, and encourage Disha to see a doctor or counsellor if it keeps going.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when Disha snapped?
qa.a: Mehak looked startled and then quiet, so she may have felt hurt or confused, yet she followed Disha to check on her.

grounding: An observer watches Disha's tired face and short answers over the exam month and Mehak's support.

passage:
Week one. Deepak started his final-year project on top of a part-time job. He told Mahima, his flatmate, he was fine. His shoulders were tight and he answered in single words.

Week four. He now snapped over small things: the dishes, the fan. He'd stopped cooking and skipped a friend's birthday. Mahima said gently, "You've been carrying a lot. I'm not saying you're wrong to be irritated. Can I do something?" He almost cried.

Week six. Deepak booked a counsellor at the health centre and handed two shifts to a coworker. He slept properly for the first time in a while. He told Mahima he was going to say sorry for the dishes, and she said there was no need.

qa.q: What did Deepak stop doing by week four?
qa.a: He stopped cooking.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling by week four, and how could Mahima tell?
qa.a: He was under heavy strain, shown by snapping over small things, skipping a birthday and almost crying when she offered help.

qa.q: What steps helped Deepak?
qa.a: He accepted support, booked a counsellor, handed two shifts to a coworker and rested.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt seeing Deepak's stress build?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and wanted to help without blaming him, as her gentle offer shows.

grounding: Deepak shows sustained stress through short answers and irritability, and rest and support follow.

passage: Harsha, you think nobody notices when you're worn out. Let your Rafiq chacha tell you about my own bad year. I was twenty-one, working at a garage in Bhopal by day and studying for a diploma by night, while my father was in and out of hospital. For three months I snapped at everyone. My face went grey. I answered my mother in single words. I thought I was hiding it. My friend Sameer finally sat me down at the chai stall. "You've been like this since March. Not one day, but months." I laughed it off. He didn't. "Go see the doctor at the clinic. Just to talk." I didn't want to. But I went. The doctor listened and told me to sleep more, drop one shift, and talk to a counsellor at the hospital where my father was. I did. It took weeks, but the grey went out of my face. Rest isn't weakness, beta.

qa.q: Where did young Rafiq work by day?
qa.a: At a garage in Bhopal.

qa.q: How was young Rafiq feeling during those three months?
qa.a: He was worn out and stressed, snapping at everyone and answering in single words, though he thought he was hiding it.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Rafiq?
qa.a: Sameer refused to let him laugh it off and urged him to see the doctor, who advised rest, fewer shifts and counselling.

qa.q: How did Sameer see Rafiq's months of irritability?
qa.a: He saw it as a long-lasting sign of strain, not a bad day, that needed rest and help.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose weeks of stress show as a grey face, short answers and irritability, and how rest and help relieve it.

passage: Varun had been working double shifts at the call centre for five weeks, covering for a colleague on leave, while finishing his final-year project. His flatmate Sarita noticed the signs: dark circles, one-word replies, snapping when she asked about dinner. Tonight he came home at midnight, slammed his bag down and said, "Don't talk to me." Sarita didn't argue. The next morning, with only ten minutes before he left, she made him tea and said, "Varun, you've been like this for weeks. Not a bad day. Weeks." He stared at the tea. "I can't stop. The project's due in two weeks." "Then can you drop one shift? Or ask your project guide for help?" He was quiet. "I'm so tired, Sarita." "I know. There's a counsellor at your college, too." That evening he told his team lead he'd do single shifts only, and booked a slot with the counsellor for Thursday.

qa.q: How long had Varun been working double shifts?
qa.a: For five weeks.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he admitted "I'm so tired"?
qa.a: He was exhausted and overwhelmed after weeks of double shifts and project work.

qa.q: What steps helped Varun lighten the load?
qa.a: Dropping to single shifts and booking a counsellor, after Sarita named the pattern of weeks.

qa.q: How did Sarita read Varun's snapping?
qa.a: She saw it as a sign of weeks of strain, not personal rudeness, so she didn't argue and spoke to him calmly.

grounding: Shows a young adult carrying stress for weeks, visible in tiredness and irritability, and responding with rest and support.

passage: In the Kolkata design office, Arnab noticed that his colleague Naveen had stopped joining the lunch table weeks ago. His face was drawn every day now, not just on deadline days. He answered questions with "Hmm" or "Later", and twice he snapped at the intern over small things. Arnab wasn't sure what was going on. It could be family, work, health. On Friday, he asked Naveen to step out for chai. "I'm not trying to pry. You've seemed really tired for a while. Weeks. Is it work?" Naveen rubbed his eyes. "It's my mother's illness. I've been driving to Howrah every night." "That's a lot." Arnab paused. "Can you tell the manager? And our company has a counselling line." Naveen nodded slowly. "I didn't think anyone noticed." On Monday he told the manager, who gave him flexible hours for a month.

qa.q: Where had Naveen been driving every night?
qa.a: To Howrah.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling during those weeks?
qa.a: He was exhausted and strained from his mother's illness, which showed in his drawn face and snapping.

qa.q: What did Arnab do that helped?
qa.a: He named the long-lasting signs gently, asked privately, and suggested telling the manager and using the counselling line.

qa.q: How did the manager respond when Naveen explained?
qa.a: The manager gave him flexible hours for a month.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a colleague's weeks-long tiredness and irritability and encouraging rest and support.

passage:
Outside the photocopy shop, Binita caught up with Rekha. "You snapped at the photocopy uncle just now. That's not you."
"I'm fine."
"You've said 'I'm fine' for five weeks. You look exhausted. You answer everything in two words."
Rekha was silent for a long moment. "Papa's been in and out of hospital since August. I do the nights with him, then come to college. I can't remember the last time I slept properly."
"Five weeks of that. No wonder."
"I thought if I just pushed through the semester..."
"What if you didn't do it all alone? Could your brother take two nights a week?"
"He's offered. I kept saying no."
"Say yes. And the college counsellor has evening slots. Would you go if I walked you there tomorrow after lab?"
"...Okay. I'll message my brother tonight."
"And right now you're napping in the library reading room while I copy your notes."
Rekha laughed for the first time in days. "Bossy."
"Caring. Same thing."

qa.q: Since when has Rekha's Papa been in and out of hospital?
qa.a: Since August.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling behind the short answers and snapping?
qa.a: Exhaustion and strain from five weeks of nights caring for Papa on top of college, feelings Rekha had been hiding behind "I'm fine".

qa.q: Which steps did Binita suggest?
qa.a: Accepting the brother's offer of two nights a week, visiting the college counsellor together, and a nap in the reading room right away.

qa.q: How had Binita been seeing Rekha over those weeks?
qa.a: As not like Rekha at all: tired-faced, curt and snapping, which worried Binita enough to name the pattern.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult carrying weeks of stress that shows as a tired face, short answers and irritability, and a friend steering them toward rest, support and counselling.
